utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sir, would you be kind enough to take the card and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. While he makes himself comfortable, may we acknowledge your return, Mr. Vasic, and we are delighted you've been able to rejoin us. You're looking so trim and fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for the concern that you and my learned friends from the Prosecution and the Defence expressed during my stay at the hospital. I am here now and Mr. Domazet and I will do our best to conclude as efficiently and as speedily as possible our part of the proceedings. We have already considered some questions, witness list and other issues, and I can inform you that we will reduce both the amount of hours and the number of witnesses. This witness will be taken by Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that's good news but we will leave it for a few days, toward the end of this week, just to give you time to settle in and to have some discussions with your fellow Defence counsel before we go to that seriously but I'm sure that both your client and Mr. Domazet rejoice with us at your return. Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was my mistake, Mr. Weiner, born out of confusion and habit. We saw so much of the Prosecution I can't believe they've finished. Mr. Domazet, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Reljic. I will be leading the examination in chief on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Mrksic. And right at the outset I would like to ask you to always pause before answering my questions. You can, if you wish, follow on the screen and as soon as you see that the interpreters have completed interpreting the question, you can proceed with your answer. Would you please at the beginning give us your personal details, dates of birth, place of birth, where you lived and so on.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of August 1948 in Drenova, Prijepolje municipality, Republic of Serbia. I completed secondary military school in Rijeka, and Titograd or Podgorica, as it is now known. Initially, I was a sergeant and as such, I was assigned to the Belgrade garrison in 1966. In 1976, after completing certain training, which was called course for officers and non-commissioned officers in driving automobiles and motorcycles, I was assigned to the Guards Brigade, to the special auto company of the Guards Brigade. Its main task was to provide security and to escort the president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito. We were assigned to take care of all the driving needs of the president. I remained there throughout my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. So you were in the unit which provided security and escort to the then president of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito. I assume that after his death, you remained in that unit, correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did your unit have the same tasks following Tito's death when new presidents came to power?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The unit continued implementing the same tasks, but in this case, we were assigned to the president of the Presidency of the SFRY. We also implemented these tasks when various guests arrived. Perhaps I omitted to mention in my previous answer that during Tito's life, we also escorted, accompanied and secured various guests, heads of state that came to visit Tito in Yugoslavia. So after Tito's death we continued performing the same type of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. You performed these tasks over a number of years. I'm now interested specifically in 1991. That year, just before the events in Vukovar, which unit were you assigned to and what was your unit doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Just before the Vukovar events, my unit existed and worked under normal circumstances. We performed the tasks that I have already described. It is generally known that as the events in the then Yugoslavia unfolded, the job that we performed was reduced in scope because the number of foreign statesmen visiting Yugoslavia decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that fully. However, you remained in that unit and in 1991 you were serving in that unit, correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember when the Guards Motorised Brigade or one of its parts went to the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that when the Guards Brigade went to the Vukovar area. Perhaps I don't have the exact date because it was quite a long time ago. However, I remember well when they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you personally deployed then with the Guards Brigade or did you have some other tasks, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I, or rather, my unit did not go to the Vukovar area. Rather, we remained in the barracks. My entire unit was on active duty in the barracks under the so-called barracks conditions. That means that all of us were in the barracks available at all times to the command, 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Reljic, when you say that you were available 24 hours a day, does this mean that all of you, including yourself personally, stayed in the barracks day and night, 24 hours a day, actively serving?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We were there day and night. Those who were not on duty were able to rest during the night. All of this means that we slept in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your commander at the time, or rather the commander of the entire Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: At that time, my commander, the commander of the entire Guards Brigade, was Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on your recollections, did he go to the Vukovar area with the Guards Brigade when it was deployed?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that's how it was, and it is generally specified by the military rules that once the unit sets off somewhere, the commander goes with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During the events in Vukovar, did your commander, Colonel Mrksic, come to Belgrade? Do you remember anything about it?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. When he came to Belgrade, during his stay there, I was his driver. That is to say, I would pick him up and drive him around Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that first. Do you remember the reasons for his trips to Belgrade? Why did Colonel Mrksic come to Belgrade in those days?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I can suppose why Colonel Mrksic used to come. It's not that I'm assuming this. I can claim this with full certainty. Because on the following day, Colonel Mrksic and other commanders attended a meeting at the then Federal Secretariat for National Defence, headed by the federal secretary for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Reljic. You said that it was on the following day that they were received. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Well, it means this: I told you that I picked up Colonel Mrksic and that I drove him, but that's not exactly how it was. I actually drove him on the following day, if I can put it that way. However, on the previous day, I completed a driving assignment for Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean the day before the reception at the office of the federal secretary, correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can now give us more details. How did this come about? What exactly did you do and who told you to do that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: This is how it was. The day before the reception held by the federal secretary, in the evening hours, the phone rang, and I answered. This was in the premises or, rather, in our duty room. Colonel Mrksic told me, "Nele, would you please go with a car to JNA boulevard?" I don't remember the number of the house. The JNA boulevard is the longest street in Belgrade. He gave me the house number. And he asked me to go look for his sister Nada, who was staying at that address, and to drive her back to his apartment. As far as I can remember, that was in the evening hours. During those days, all of us, Serbs and Yugoslavs, regardless of whether we were involved in politics or not, invariably watched the main news programme on television and closely followed all events, including war events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That was typical for that period of time, and I remember this well. The main TV news programme called Dnevnik would normally last half an hour but sometimes, and rather frequently, it would last much longer, an hour to two hours, in view of numerous news reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So based on what you remember, sometime on that day, as you were watching the news programme, you received this order to go to this address. Do you remember what this place was called where you went to fetch the sister?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Since this is a very long street, JNA boulevard, which still is known under that name even near Avalski Put, a hill near Belgrade, I tried to determine where that house number is located, and this is how I learned that this house is right across a well-known restaurant at the time called Zupa, and near a post office. So I got into the car and went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you locate the sister of Colonel Mrksic at that address?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I found her there. I remember that evening. It was already dark. I told you that that street is very long, and the road is quite dangerous, has many curves. As I was driving I saw the house number and it was right in the middle of a curve, curving right. As I told you, that road is very dangerous and it doesn't have a shoulder where one can park. It has a very narrow area right next to the road. I was being extremely careful and I parked my car on the right side, on this basically non-existing shoulder, doing my best not to cause a traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And how did you find the sister?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Once I found the house with the right number, I parked the car, and as I was leaving the car, a woman emerged from a bungalow-type house. If I may say so, I was surprised by the appearance of that woman. In my view, she was very distressed. She was almost crying and screaming, and she dashed towards me saying, "Mile, Mile." I realised that she thought that I was Mile or perhaps she thought that Mile had come with me. So I told her, "Madam, please settle down. I will take you now to your brother Mile."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did she have any belongings to take with her? And did you set out towards the Mrksic residence?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. She had two bags with her, full of things, and as I came closer to her, intending to help her carry the bags, I realised that she had obviously suffered a lot and that she was under severe stress. She was, if I may say so, quite disheveled in her appearance, and her clothing, which made me think that she had experienced some very unusual circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you were driving towards the Mrksic residence, did you talk to her about anything or not?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I mostly didn't talk to her so as not to irritate her. When she kept asking me, "Where is Mile, where is Mile?" I would simply tell her, "Madam, please calm down, we are on our way to your brother's and we will get there in about ten minutes or so."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Of course, since I knew where Colonel Mrksic lived, I went there, parked the car and took the bags from the lady, and asked her to come with me. And this is what she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you take her things and accompany her to the Mrksic apartment and then can you please describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Of course. I took her things and already in the corridor upstairs, you could hear, because Mile knew she was coming, he opened the door and I brought in the things to the apartment and Madam Nada also entered Colonel Mrksic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you stay in this apartment or not for sometime?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in the apartment for a short amount of time with Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And can you describe how this happened, any initiative and what you did, what you discussed?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: My unit, let me say, was always a highly professional unit, which, amongst other tasks, also carried out driving assignments. So whenever we had that kind of situation, we would do the assignment, of course, then we would say hello or good-bye and then return to the unit. Then, of course, Colonel Mrksic, Mile, insisted on such occasion, and he said, "Nele, please sit down. And he said, "Nele, please sit down. Would you like to have a drink or something to refresh yourself?" And I sat down and I think that I had a couple of sips of wine or a glass -- a couple of sips, I think, as I was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described earlier your first meeting with Mile Mrksic's sister and what your impression was. You probably saw their encounter and can you please tell us how that was?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The encounter in those circumstances was not very emotional, I can say, and as a person, I was bothered. I wanted to find out what it was that happened to Madam Nada, what was going on, because already when I met her she had gone to the bathroom with Mile's wife, and I asked, "What is it with Nada? What's the matter with her? What was it that happened to her?" Colonel Mrksic told me that -- I mean, what can I do when she went over to the other side? It was all clear to me, and I didn't ask anything else. But still I was curious why that person was in that state, which is why I asked Mile about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, "In that state," you mean the first time you saw -- you saw her when she reacted nervously, that she behaved the same way when she entered the Mrksic's household. Could you please clarify that a little bit more for us?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a state of, let me say it was a particular kind of state of mind, with a sort of negative emotional charge. That's the state Madam Nada was in, in relation to Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "negative emotional charge," what do you mean? Was that some kind of hysterical episode or something like that? Could you please try to explain your impressions a little more of how it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Just the fact that when I met her for the first time, she was shouting and screaming, "Where is Mile? Why didn't he come to get me?" And this again actually happened or transpired when they met, and it was evident that the sister was in some way dissatisfied with her brother Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That is what your opinion was based on her general behaviour, is that how we can understand that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you didn't talk with her any more or see her any more during that brief time you spent sitting with Mrksic? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct because she went to the bathroom, and probably she needed to do that because of the state she was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you didn't stay there for a long time. Can you please tell us how long you actually stayed there and then what you did after that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: From what I can recall, I stayed there maybe for ten or 15 minutes at the most. That's how long I stayed in Colonel Mrksic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Before I left, before we said good-bye, Mile Mrksic told me that, he told me the following: "Nele, come to see me tomorrow at such and such a time, and you're going to drive me." For me, the most important thing was to know the time that I was to pick him up. I remembered that and I wrote it down. We said our good-byes and I went to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the next day, did you come as agreed the day before? Did you come to collect him?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I came the next day to pick him up at the agreed-upon time, and I took Mile to the Guards Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, "At the time agreed the day before," you mean the time that he set or do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The time that he said I should get there and I'm sure that that's how it was. I really couldn't be specific and tell you what time it actually was but it was definitely the time that he set. It was sometime in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, "Morning," it could be early morning, late morning. Can you be more specific whether it was early in the morning or --

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Well, I could be almost sure that it was between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And after that, do you remember, after you dropped him off at the barracks, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Once again, according to an order by Colonel Mrksic, I took the car to Heliodrom to wait for a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who were you supposed to pick up?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to pick up Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you pick him up?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went there and I waited for the helicopter. Major Tesic came out of the helicopter, and I also brought him to the command. I was closeby and waited because I knew that I would be taking Colonel Mrksic to other places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you take him anywhere else, and where did you take him?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: After I brought Major Tesic there, and after some time, perhaps some 20 minutes or so, Colonel Mrksic and Major Tesic came out and they went and sat in the car and Colonel Mrksic said, "Nele, take us to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence," which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you wait for Colonel Mrksic in your car or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I waited for him because that was his order, to wait for him. So I waited in the car at the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And which building was that, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. It's the A building of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. The car was parked at the parking, which is between building 1 of the General Staff and building A. That's where the car was, while I waited in a room close to the reception desk of building A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any other drivers there, other senior officers, or were you there by yourself?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I remember well that there, in that room, there was also General Biorcevic's driver with me and we were waiting there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And do you remember what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: After a certain amount of time, Colonel Mrksic came out with Major Tesic and in accordance with their orders, I took them to the Guards hall which is at Topcider. Actually I took them to the restaurant in the Guards hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Even though it might be clear from your answer, but still I would like to ask you whether this was a military restaurant, whether it belonged to the army?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. It was run by the Dedinje military institution. Actually, that institution was in charge of all the military restaurants and mess halls.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, and it was in the area of Belgrade called Topcider?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened then? Did you stay there also to wait for Colonel Mrksic or did you do something else?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed there in the restaurant. The restaurant has a number of sections, number of rooms, so I was in a different room, and at one point, Colonel Mrksic came out and told me that I should take Major Tesic to his apartment. He lived in New Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, before this thing that Colonel Mrksic was there for, Major Tesic left that gathering; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Major Tesic was at that gathering for a very short period of time and I assume that he wanted to go and see his family. I drove him to his address in New Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember taking him right to his house and do you recall that it was his house or his apartment that you took him to?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No. I took him close to his apartment, and I have to tell this: There was an incident when the father saw his son at the children's playground where the child was playing, and when he saw that his father was coming, the child ran and hugged him, and, of course, they both hugged each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, so when you said you didn't take Major Tesic to his house, you actually left him at the place where he saw his son or you went all the way to his apartment?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The drive was finished, as far as Major Tesic was concerned, and, of course, I had to return to the Guards hall in order to wait for Colonel Mrksic, which is what I did. I went back to the Guards hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. And does that mean that that day, you needed to be wherever Colonel Mrksic needed to be?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day, I was practically inseparable from Colonel Mrksic, because I was driving him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And do you remember how late you finished with your duties that day?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that there was a formal lunch, and the way it was, it was a formal lunch and a formal dinner, and since it's in my nature, I'm like that, I was there, then I went outside, I walked around and waited in the car or near the car, but Colonel Mrksic came after me and he said, "Nele, did you eat anything?" And I said, "Colonel." And he said, "Nele, you have to go inside." And then he took me by the arm and took me inside and he told the staff there to give this man lunch, meaning me. So I had lunch there and then I continued to wait for the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After all of these duties that Colonel Mrksic had, do you remember where and when you took him after it was all over at the end of that day?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: After all those activities there, I took Colonel Mrksic and another officer further, and I remember that very well because there is a large parking lot in front of the Guards Brigade and there is also a street that is quite steep that goes from there, so when I left in the car, it was already evening. From the other direction, from the top down, down from the hill, a vehicle passed by at quite great speed. It wasn't anything critical but there was a kind of brief encounter there. So I remember it because of that. And in any case, we took some shortcuts from the Guards hall through the barracks and we took a shortcut and came to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. And then did you finally take Colonel Mrksic home that evening or did someone else do that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: When we came to the brigade headquarters, there was a car waiting somewhere close with an officer who entered the Guards hall together with Colonel Mrksic and that officer then came out of the car. I took Colonel Mrksic to his house. I took him to his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And can you tell us what time of day it was or approximately what time it was when you did this?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I remember it was dark already, it was evening, it was already evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. And when you left Colonel Mrksic, did he give you any instructions what to do further? Did he ask you to do anything else?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: When I left Colonel Mrksic, he told me, "Nele, be at my place tomorrow morning." And he set the time. And I remember that this was somewhat earlier, so it was perhaps approximately at 7.00, something like that, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say 7.00, do you mean that that was the time he told you to be there at his place?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Absolutely. That is the time he asked me to come the following day, in front of his apartment, to be in front of his apartment at 7.00 the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And were you there the next morning in front of his apartment?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I did come. In any case, when we are doing something like that, we like to make sure and leave some extra time so we are always there earlier than we are supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you believe that you were there shortly before 7.00 and was that when Colonel Mrksic came to the car?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I waited. The time came. However, Colonel Mrksic did not come out. Naturally, I continued to wait. 15 minutes or 20 minutes passed and I saw that something wasn't quite right, simply that the colonel wasn't there so I was thinking what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Then a girl, a young girl, came out of the entrance to Colonel Mrksic's building. She came to the car and she asked, "Are you waiting for Colonel Mrksic?" I said, "Yes." And she said, "You can go. You can go ahead and go to the barracks. Colonel Mrksic has gone to headquarters with his own car." And then she went somewhere. I got into the car and I went and I seem to recall that I stopped and -- because I didn't know this young girl, I asked her, "Where are you going?" She said, "I'm going to school." And I said, "Why don't you come in the car and I will take you to school." She was reluctant and I said, "No, you can come. I'll drop you off. I'm going in that direction any way." So she got in the car and I took her to town, to her school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember where you took her?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well. That was the area around Kalinic market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last two pages of testimony concern this witness's visit to the defendant Mrksic on the 22nd. It is in direct contrast or direct conflict with the notes that were provided to us pursuant to 65 ter. The notes which were provided to us on August 10th, on August 25th, August 29th and September 1st. I just want an objection on the record. We haven't received any proofing notes and there is a direct conflict because in the notes here, it says, on the 22nd November 1991, he drove Colonel Mrksic to the military airport where from Colonel Mrksic left with Major Tesic to Negoslavci. There is nothing about this situation at the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the note, the summary, reflects that on the 22nd, in the morning, the driver was there. Colonel Mrksic left Belgrade on that day in a helicopter. He travelled to Negoslavci. However, the witness stated today and also yesterday or rather the day before yesterday, when I saw him for the first time, this witness told me that it was the way he described it to us today, namely that he didn't drive Colonel Mrksic on that day because Colonel Mrksic had already gone out earlier on his own. So unfortunately, we didn't know this when we wrote the summary on this specific issue. This is precisely why I put this question to the witness so that we could clarify it while he's still here. So can I ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the 22nd, did you drive Colonel Mrksic? So this is the day after the events in the Guards hall in Belgrade? Did you take him anywhere, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No, on the last day I didn't drive Colonel Mrksic anywhere. I just drove his daughter to her school, as I've explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you were supposed to drive him, you were scheduled to drive him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in every case in this Tribunal, if there is different evidence coming, proofing notes are supplied, and I think for this case as well as all the other cases in the Tribunal, proofing notes should be supplied from this day on. If there is new information, if there are new facts, if they are in conflict with the summary, counsel must provide proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Defence counsel will take notice of that, and Mr. Domazet and Mr. Vasic in particular, during their case. Carry on, please, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So on the 22nd, in the morning, you didn't see Colonel Mrksic? The last time you saw him was the previous night, correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So from that day until the Guards Brigade returned to Belgrade, did Colonel Mrksic come to Belgrade again?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Mrksic didn't come until the Guards Brigade returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how long it was before the entire brigade returned to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: A brief period of time, several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another question: When you described the events of that day, when you drove Colonel Mrksic first to the Federal Secretariat and then to Topcider, you described to us what happened that day. Do you remember which day it was?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The day when I drove Colonel Mrksic is the day I remember quite well. I know very well which date it was. Shall I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please. Tell us what date it was and how come you remember it so well.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There was the reception at the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. All Yugoslav radio stations, Serbian radio stations announced and even some international radio stations made an announcement. In addition to this, I have another recollection. Serbs, as a rule, celebrate their patron saint days. A friend of mine, on that day, celebrated his patron saint day, which is St. Archangel. And it happened to be on that day. As to how I remember this, I remember it because I was supposed to go to my friend's house on the account of him celebrating his patron saint day and I was supposed to go even though we were on 24-hour duty in the barracks, and I wasn't really supposed to leave the barracks. It was against the rules. But I thought that I could still go to my friend's house but upon obtaining consent from my superiors. However, after I started driving on that day, it did not even occur to me to go and ask for approval to go to my friend's house. In the end, my friend was quite angry at me for not coming on that day, even though for decades prior to that, I invariably went to his house on his patron saint day. Naturally, I couldn't explain to him the reasons why I didn't come that year, but I remember that he was quite offended and it almost cost me his friendship.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are sure that the reception at the federal secretary of Defence and everything else that happened that day was on the day of St. Archangel, the Orthodox holiday, correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, that's precisely why I remember. That's the main reason I remember that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is one of Orthodox Serbian holidays. Is it a holiday celebrated by many people or by few people?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I think that St. Archangel Michael, is the second-most-celebrated Serbian orthodox holiday, if we look at the number of families celebrating that day. I think that the most celebrated patron saint day is St. Nicholas day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what date it is, the St. Archangel Michael day?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. I know that. That's the 21st of November. That's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you testified about the reception at the federal secretary of Defence and all the other tasks you had that day with Colonel Mrksic was on that date. As for the events surrounding the sister of Colonel Mrksic, what date was that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Given that we know the date of St. Archangel Michael day, it is easy to conclude which date it was when I drove the sister of Colonel Mrksic. It was on the previous day and it's also easy to conclude which date it was when I was supposed to drive Colonel Mrksic again, on the following day, the day following St. Archangel Michael day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, okay? Now, sir, I just want to start by asking you that you were first contacted about this matter about three weeks ago, four weeks ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I haven't received an answer?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were contacted by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were asked about your activities over a period of three or four days, a period of three or four days in November of 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you've never testified previously about any of these facts, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I have never testified previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've never been interviewed previously about any of these facts; isn't that correct, other than most recently, three weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No. But the first contact with the Defence, that is to say with the lawyer, specifically Mr. Vasic, was several years ago, if I can put it that way. The first contact wasn't just two or three weeks ago. Our contact of a few weeks ago wasn't the first one. The first contact was two or three years ago, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to that, no one had ever questioned you previously about these facts, prior to let's say three years ago, prior to 2003?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And throughout the 1990s, no one ever asked you to write a report, interviewed you or interrogated you about these facts?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me to write anything or sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, since we are dealing with facts which occurred over a three-day period almost 15 years ago, did you keep a diary indicating what you did on each of these days?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I personally never kept a diary about those days or any other days during my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in addition to a diary, you don't have a calendar or an agenda listing what you did on each of those days in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No. I don't have a calendar. I never kept anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically -- well, let's add: There are no logs or any writings as to who you drove during that time period of November 1991; isn't that correct too?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: If those records exist, they are not available to me. I actually think that no such records exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically we are relying on your memory alone as to what occurred 15 years ago, since there are no writings?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you served as a driver, you said from 1976 to what year? To what date were you a driver in the Guards motorised brigade? You didn't indicate your date of retirement.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I retired, I went into retirement, in 1998 to 1999. My service was terminated that year on new years day, between 1998 and 1999, that is to say on the 31st of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in all those years, you've never maintained a list of the persons that you drove and the specific dates and times?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: That's another matter. As I said to you, in accordance with the rules that existed at the time, and regulations in the army, all our sorties with a vehicle had to be recorded in the records of the fleet, the fleet of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you don't have this list, do you?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that list, and I'm not authorised to have it. I'm just a driver. I simply don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having been a driver so many years you really couldn't say how many people or how many trips you had made over the years, how many people you have driven or how many trips you've made? You've made hundreds, if not thousands.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: One could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you probably couldn't state how many trips you made in November 1991 in total, not having any records.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I could state, based on my recollections, that in November of 1991, I had such and such number of assignments, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But could you state an exact number?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Not with accuracy, because it's been many years, and it's hard to remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And being hard to remember everything, you couldn't state who you drove that month at which times. You couldn't say at each date I drove these particular people and at exactly these times because it's almost 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By the way, you referred to St. -- was it St. Michael's day? The Archangel's day being on the 21st of November. Do you know what day that was, what day of the week? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. It was on a Thursday. Now, you knew who Colonel Mrksic was as your commander?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you said you knew him well, in fact, he didn't call you sergeant, he called you Nele instead of your first name Nenad; isn't that correct? Your nickname, he addressed you by?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. My name is Nele.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the documents provided to the Court and to the Prosecution, it has your name as Nenad. That's incorrect? Nenad, N-E-N-A-D, Reljic. That's not your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No. My name is Nele Reljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you knew Colonel Mrksic well. Had you ever driven him previously or prior to November 1991?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I most likely drove him sometimes, not frequently but sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew where his home was. You drove right to his home. Had you been to his home previously? Or after November 1991, have you been to his home?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No, no. Never prior to the days I described, or rather, prior to the evening I described when I took the sister. I never went to his apartment prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever drive or were you ever assigned to drive from Belgrade to Vukovar or from Vukovar back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There were driving assignments but what do you mean, specifically what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was interested in the time. It's 155 kilometres, approximately 155 kilometres from Vukovar to Belgrade. What's the approximate time to drive that distance? Being a driver for many years.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Depending on the vehicle you are using. If you're travelling in a passenger vehicle, then naturally you would arrive earlier. If you're driving in an all-terrain vehicle or in a truck or in a bus, that will change the driving time. But let's say that you're travelling in a passenger car. It would take about two hours of normal driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we go to November of 1991, where we know there were check-points along the road way, you would have to stop. We are dealing with a two to two plus hour trip, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: One could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because with the checkpoints and we are not dealing with highways, it's not a quick trip of let's say an hour and a half. It's a longer trip.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The major part of that road is on the highway, and then the rest are just national roads and other categories of roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But as I said in November 1991, where there were check-points set up along the way we would be dealing with a two to two-plus hour trip in a passenger car, especially with check-points, where you would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please? It wasn't picked up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more issue to address. Would you like me to do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Now, you testified that you did not drive Colonel Mrksic on November 22nd 1991. You testified to that earlier today. Do you recall testifying to that about 40 minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you had previously met with Defence counsel you said around 2003, so you said two to three years ago, so 2003, 2004. Did you tell them at that time about the events of those days in November of 1991? Did you provide your knowledge to them back then, some years ago?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. Most likely we did talk about it but I can't tell you that for sure right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 10th of August 2006, the Defence filed a summary of your testimony, and on the bottom line it says, on 22 November 1991, he, meaning you, drove Colonel Mrksic to the military airport, and that's on page 13 of the 65 ter(G) submission. Now, did you provide that information to the Defence, that on the 22nd of November, you drove Colonel Mrksic to the military airport?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, I'll read the whole thing. "On the 22nd November 1991, he drove Colonel Mrksic to the military airport in Batajnica where from Colonel Mrksic left with Major Tesic to Negoslavci." Did you provide that information which is listed under your name as a summary of your testimony? Did you provide that information to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that I did because this is not materially true, that I drove Colonel Mrksic on the 22nd. I remember when I did drive him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you said today that you just notified Defence counsel three days or so ago that you didn't drive Colonel Mrksic on November 22nd. So if you didn't tell them about that back then, who would have told them?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know who could have said that on my behalf. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you believe counsel is just making that up and putting that under your name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's going too far, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Withdrawn, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you said for the first time three days ago that you didn't drive Colonel Mrksic on the 22nd. Was there any reason that you told Defence three days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, this is a careful point where there is a danger that in giving voice to what I suspect may be your objection, you will in fact unwittingly no doubt be assisting the witness. So I would ask you to wait for the moment until the questions are answered. Then you can make whatever point it is you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, is there any reason that you notified counsel only recently, only three days ago, that you did not drive Colonel Mrksic on November 22nd 1991?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There is absolutely no reason why I should not tell them that I did not drive him because I did not drive him on that day. I drove him on the 21st. I was supposed to drive him on the 22nd but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you just suddenly realise this fact a few days ago? And today, to notify the Court?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I have no reason, and I did not have any reason to realise that fact, because it was always the fact that I drove Colonel Mrksic on the 21st, the whole day, and that I was supposed to drive him on the 22nd but I did not do so and I described why I did not drive him. That is that he used his own transport to go, to reach the headquarters or the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he used his own transport after notifying you to be present at 7.00 in the morning on that date?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I assume that he used his own transport. Sometimes he had the habit of just getting into his car and driving himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he didn't then notify you first thing in the morning not to appear, so he wouldn't be wasting your time?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Mrs. Mrksic testified a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're not aware that she testified a few days ago, on August 30th, I'm sorry, yes, August 30th, that you did not drive Colonel Mrksic to the airport on that morning? Are you aware that she testified to that?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. I did not have the opportunity to meet Mrs. Mrksic, not even when I was in their apartment. We did not -- we were introduced to each other, as would be the proper formal thing to do. Even when I was at the apartment when I brought Colonel Mrksic's sister we were not introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you realise that her testimony on August 30th is in conflict with the factual summary that you were going to say that you did drive Colonel Mrksic to the airport, that there is a direct conflict between that factual summary and her testimony?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know when Mrs. Mrksic testified and what her testimony was. I really don't know that. I didn't even have the occasion to formally be introduced to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, it's nothing more than a coincidence that she testifies a few days ago that you didn't not drive her husband to the airport, and instead, you offered to take her daughter to school, and today, you testify in conflict with the 65 ter summary and say the same thing? Is that just a coincidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There is no coincidence there. I know, when I would go on a driving assignment, when I complete the assignment and when I -- I know when I would complete an assignment and I know when it could not be completed because Colonel Mrksic had already left with his own car. I assume that he used his own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you were doing nothing more today than tailoring your testimony to help your friend, Colonel Mrksic, tailoring your testimony to Mrs. Mrksic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There is absolutely no tailoring. What I have already said, and explained, is absolutely true. It's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, do you have any submission or do you just want to go into re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to explain why I made the objection. I wanted to object because the witness did not say. I said that the witness told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, if you are going to put questions to the witness about this matter, can I suggest you should do that first rather than you give some version of what happened yourself. And you can put your submission later. You understand the point. There is a point being made of credibility. It's better to test it through the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I actually understood that I should explain my objection first. I was waiting for the end of the cross-examination. But of course I'm going to put my questions first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Weiner asked you about your contacts with the Defence and he meant that in the plural, contacts with Defence attorneys. You were talking about Mr. Vasic actually?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My direct question is: I, as a Defence attorney, did you know me before now?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I never met you before and the first time we met was some two days ago, here in The Hague. Before that, I had never seen you or been introduced to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We spoke here in The Hague. Did I ask you to tell me how everything was and then you told me about the events as you recalled them?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I absolutely told you about the events based on how I remember them, and because the things that happened were specific, and since I did drive the commander for those thee days, or, rather, I did drive him, so I remember everything. It's all crystal clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what you told me, is that what you've also told us here in your testimony before this Trial Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Including what you said that on the 22nd you did not drive Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation is quite clear. I was told, and I was supposed to drive Colonel Mrksic on the 22nd, but in view of the fact that he had already left, I didn't drive him. I assumed that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner asked you about how long it takes to drive from Vukovar to Belgrade, and he said that there were also check-points there and that sometime was lost if you stopped at the check-points. So what I wanted to ask you is: What is the distance from Belgrade to Sid?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The distance between Belgrade and Sid is approximately 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the highway or just a regular road?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: This is a modern highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I say the highway, or the motorway, what I mean is that are there at least two lanes for traffic for each direction?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what is the distance between Sid and Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: If the distance to Sid is approximately 100 kilometres, then there is about 50 or 60 more kilometres to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, so is Negoslavci before Vukovar, because you said it's 150 kilometres from Belgrade to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't understand the gentleman actually who was asking this question. I was driving to Negoslavci. I would usually go to Negoslavci. So I never went to Vukovar. So I'm not sure about the distance. Perhaps if you just deduct or -- the difference from the distance that I've already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because of the check-points from Belgrade to Vukovar, the distance can be covered in two to two and a half hours, and if the highway to -- from Belgrade to Sid is used, and then from Belgrade to Sid, it's about 100 kilometres, then how long does it take to cover this distance from Sid to Belgrade without stopping for any other reason other than to stop at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The road -- the highway from Sid to Belgrade, when there is no traffic, when it's not crowded, it's something that can be covered pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that there is no traffic, what you're trying to say is that at the time it was very light traffic?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: There was practically no traffic on that highway in that section at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And can you please tell me what is the maximum speed permitted on that road?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: The maximum speed permitted is something that I assume is in most highways in the world, and that is 120 kilometres an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So a vehicle, passenger vehicle, going from Sid to Belgrade, how long would it need going at that speed?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: A more powerful passenger vehicle could cover that distance comfortably in an hour, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you about Sid and this because the distance is not quite reliable, but it's easy to establish that and I don't see any particular point in doing that. When you responded to Mr. Weiner's question about records, you said that you did not keep any records or a diary or any notes. Does that refer throughout -- for the whole period of your military career or just to the period that we discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I, as a person, absolutely never kept any personal records about my work. I never did anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about the apartment house where Colonel Mrksic's apartment is, you said that you knew from before where it was but you explained that this time when you were taking his sister there, you actually entered the apartment for the first time. Did you ever before that or after that go inside the Mrksic apartment or was that the only time?

utterances.speaker: NELE RELJIC
utterances.text: I never entered Colonel Mrksic's apartment before that evening, when I helped his sister to go in, when I was helping her to take her bags. She is a woman so I wanted to help her. And in view of the state that she was in, that's what I did. I brought her things in and that was the first time that I entered Colonel Mrksic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Reljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness and if you permit me I just wanted in one sentence to explain what we talked about earlier, what was the essence of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Weiner's question was, you said earlier, that three days ago, you told the Defence that you did not drive Mrksic. The witness did not say that in this trial. I said that when I said that I got this information from the witness when I talked to the witness yesterday and the day before. Before his testimony. The witness came to The Hague on Saturday, not even three days ago but actually two days ago, and yesterday I had the opportunity to speak with him and this is exactly what he said so I said that and not the witness. So that was the gist of my objection, that the witness did not say that at all, three days ago, but that I said it. Again, I want to say that it is absolutely correct and true that in the summary I mistakenly said that he -- instead of he was supposed to drive him, that I said he did drive him. So I made the summary here in The Hague. It was supposed to be submitted by the 10th of August. So I received the information from Mr. Vasic and it was all done very quickly. I never spoke to this witness actually or to any other Defence witnesses so this is how this mistake came about. And finally, I'd like to apologise for this to the Prosecution. It is widely known that such mistakes took place before. The Prosecution itself made several similar mistakes, and the witness said to me what he basically repeated today in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Reljic, that your evidence is at an end and you are now free to leave and to return at a convenient time to your home. The Chamber would thank you for your assistance in coming here and for the evidence that you've given. You're now free to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is the first day in the courtroom for me, and my co-counsel explained to you the situation last week. The Defence has nine witnesses, each of whom has a passport ready. And we planned on submitting their passports to the Dutch embassy last week on Wednesday. However, we were told that it was impossible to submit passports directly. Rather, it needs to be done through fields officer who came last week on Friday, and took over passports. He needed prior approval of the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs in order to do that, before he travelled to Belgrade. So last week, on Thursday, we did not have the field officer in Belgrade and that's the information I received from our staff awaiting the contact with the field officer in Belgrade. The field officer is scheduled to arrive in Belgrade today and I hope that that will resolve the status of all nine witnesses. If that were indeed to take place as planned, that means that the next witness could travel to-- to arrive in The Hague tomorrow afternoon and come to the courtroom on Wednesday. The only problem that I believe we are unable to resolve in the technical sense is that we need a field officer present for each contact with the Dutch embassy, and the field officer is not available and in Belgrade every day so I think that this is the only way that is available for us in order to obtain visas for our witnesses, namely that the field officer take over all pass ports at the same time. We also need to take into account that it's not easy to get a place on a plane. The planes are full currently. And sometimes we will need to put witnesses on different airliners in order to ensure their presence here so that everything can proceed as planned. As I said, had we had direct access to the Dutch embassy, then all of the passports would have been at the Dutch embassy last week and everything would have been resolved by now. I'm afraid that due to these technical problems, we currently do not have a witness available, and if things proceed as planned, and as we were informed by the field officer and the registry, the first witness could arrive on Tuesday afternoon and be available in the courtroom on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you mentioned nine passports. Does that complete the number of passports that will be necessary for the witnesses you intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that represents 80 per cent of the witnesses that we intend to call. As for the remaining two or three witnesses, I had to meet with some of them several times prior to coming here in The Hague because they had not given their final consent to come here and testify, and they had not obtained passports. So as it stands now, I foresee that in addition to this group of nine witnesses, there will be two or three more at the most and I think that that will be the case of Mr. Mrksic. So the majority of our witnesses are the nine who are currently awaiting their visas, as I've explained to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the names of the nine?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that right away, Your Honours. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have passports for the following witnesses: Andrija Milojevic, or Milevic. Razvigor Virijevic, Velimir Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you just pause? I'm trying to pick up these people on your 65 ter list. That's numbers 2, 15 and 16, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct, Your Honours. I will give you the numbers in addition to the names so it will be easier for you to follow. 17, Dusan Jaksic, 19, Ivan Minic, 21 -- I apologise, 22, Nenad Milicevic. 31, Zoran Basic. 34, Milan Babic. I'm just verifying to see whether I omitted any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got 8 so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And Dusan Milosevic, number 21. We were supposed to get his passport yesterday and I think that it came in. Plus our expert witness, Mile Stojkovic. That would be nine. And with the witness who was supposed to hand over his passport yesterday, that would be ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So for all of those, you're dependent on visas, they each having passports at the present time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. They have their passports plus they need to provide a photograph for visa. The form for visa application is filled by somebody else and I think that visas for two witnesses are ready, Razvigor Virijevic, who is supposed to be our first witness here, and witness Coric and Basic according to the information we have also have guarantees for their visa. As for other witnesses, we will need assistance to ensure that they get their visas on time and in the meantime we'll try to do our best to ensure that their evidence doesn't take too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And there may be two or three, you said, additional, if they obtain passports?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two or three witnesses who are currently awaiting their passports. They applied for passports to be issued. That would represent about 80 per cent of our witnesses. I wanted to tell you today that based on what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ground has moved there. The 80 per cent were those that had passports, as I understood it. And then there were two or three more that were seeking passports if they gave their consent to give evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, out of 35 witnesses, which we initially put on the list, we intend to call between 15 and 17. The number of 15 to 17 witnesses can also be reduced because we are currently considering whether to call here some witnesses or not. Some witnesses have still not given us their consent to come here and testify. So the number that we have right now is 15 to 17 out of initial 35. The nine who have their passports and the three that we have already examined here is 12 altogether, nine plus three is 12, and then in addition to these 12, we would call additional three to five witnesses who still do not have their passports and who are potential witnesses. As I said to you, it could be that we will reduce this number further, the number of witnesses, but we might also reduce the number of hours scheduled for their testimony. In addition to these witnesses, we have one more expert witness who is a military expert. So the number of 15 to 17 witnesses includes the protected witness who is going to come here under subpoena, and we are not concerned with his passport naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will merely delay matters and may not be helpful at the moment for the Chamber to express its full views about the situation, Mr. Vasic. Clearly, what is needed is for the difficulty of the Defence's own making, that there are no visas and that all witnesses do not have passports, needs to be remedied as quickly as possible. The next thing that needs to be remedied is that the Prosecution needs to be given a correct order in which to expect witnesses, because the present information is clearly not now correct. The next thing is that you need to consider again the time estimates, because it is evident from the first three witnesses that you have considerably overestimated the time that will be necessary. Those things having been dealt with, you need to liaise carefully with your other lead Defence counsel so that they can plan reliably the dates upon which they need to have their witnesses here, because the information you are now providing will alter the position they anticipate considerably. The only course the Chamber can take at the moment, it appears, is to adjourn until Wednesday morning, in the hope that by then there will be witnesses here with the necessary visas, and clearly you need to give the Prosecution and the other counsel notification of who will be called and in what order, preferably today, so that they've got some chance of being ready. In view of these changes, it will clearly be at the end of this week before we can expect realistically to look at the overall programme for the Defence. It is unfortunate that there is this uncertainty and that it involves the lost time that is presently being encountered. Apart from that, the Chamber will not make any comment at the present time. For the reasons indicated, we must adjourn now until Wednesday. Should it be the case on Wednesday that your problems have not by then resolved, we will expect from you, Mr. Vasic, a very clear indication of what will be the future course of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With good fortune, they will be resolved by Wednesday and we will have witnesses, and let us hope then that other counsel are in a position to adjust to the changed plans. We will adjourn now until Wednesday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.50 p.m., to
